Zhang Xiaoxiao.lab_name: Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital, Jinan University (Guangzhou, China)
Zhang Xiaoxiao.role: Eye specialist at Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital who works on childhood myopia, from school screening and myopia-control lenses to the biology of the sclera in animal models
Zhang Xiaoxiao.sub: Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital, affiliated with Jinan University (PubMed affiliation 2023–2026) · Optometry and Strabismus Department (2023)
story: Myopia (short-sightedness) usually happens because the eyeball grows too long. The sclera, the tough white outer wall of the eye, has to remodel for that to happen. Xiaoxiao Zhang was senior author of the 2026 FASEB Journal study in this Atlas (WEN2026), which used human scleral cells and guinea pigs whose eyes were covered to induce myopia. Too much autophagy in the sclera, the cell's recycling system, appeared to link low-oxygen stress to the remodelling. Rapamycin injected under the conjunctiva made the myopia worse, the autophagy blocker 3-MA eased it, and atropine eye drops slowed it. The team measured AMPK/mTOR/P70S6K signalling, but the paper does not show that this route causes the effect, and the results come from cells and animals, not children.

A companion 2026 paper from the same Guangzhou group, again with Zhang as last author, traced the low-oxygen signal one step further: in hypoxic scleral cells and in guinea pigs, the HIF-1alpha protein pushed cells towards glycolysis and lactate production, and blocking glycolysis reduced myopic eye growth.

Much of Zhang's other published work is clinical. PubMed lists papers from Guangzhou Aier Eye Hospital on a vision screening of more than 170,000 primary school pupils in three Guangzhou districts (2025), on predicting eye growth in children wearing orthokeratology night lenses over six years (2025), on comparing two kinds of myopia-control spectacle lenses (2023), and on eyelid hygiene during orthokeratology (2026). The hospital is affiliated with Jinan University.

highlights.WEN2026: Senior author: led the guinea pig and scleral cell study linking excess scleral autophagy to myopia, in which rapamycin worsened and 3-MA eased experimental myopia.

Zhang Xiaoxiao.note: No official staff page found; position derived from PubMed affiliations only. A 2022 case report by a Xiao-Xiao Zhang at Shanghai Children's Hospital was not counted (likely a different person).

Dan L.lab_name: School of Pharmacy, Chengdu University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Dan L.role: Yeast geneticist at Chengdu University who studies reversible mutations that let cells switch drug resistance on and off, using rapamycin resistance in fission yeast as the model
Dan L.sub: School of Pharmacy and Antibiotics Innovation and Resistance Control Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu University (PubMed affiliation 2025–2026) · Life Sciences Institute, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou (Xiangwei He lab, PubMed affiliation 2021)
story: Fission yeast is a single-celled fungus used to study how cells control growth. Its TORC1 complex is the yeast version of mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and it can be blocked with rapamycin plus caffeine. Lufeng Dan is first author of the 2026 Microbiology Spectrum study in this Atlas (DAN2026). Some yeast cells became resistant to the drugs, then lost the resistance again a few generations later. The team showed that this was not an epigenetic switch. Mutations that broke the gaf1 gene appeared under drug pressure and then reverted to the normal DNA sequence when the drug was gone. Gaf1 is a GATA transcription factor that slows growth downstream of TORC1. The authors warn that such hidden switches can quietly change laboratory yeast stocks.

The paper continues a line of work Dan began at the Life Sciences Institute of Zhejiang University in Hangzhou, in the group of Xiangwei He. A 2021 PNAS paper with Dan as first author found drug-resistance mutations in fission yeast that are made by short tandem duplications of DNA and then flip back to the original sequence, and used deep genome sequencing to find thousands of such duplications in a single population.

By 2025 Dan was at the School of Pharmacy of Chengdu University, where a paper in the Chinese journal Hereditas described a screen that isolated 14 yeast strains with unstable rapamycin resistance, again with Xiangwei He as a co-author.

highlights.DAN2026: First author: showed that on-and-off resistance to TORC1 inhibitors in fission yeast comes from reversible mutations in gaf1.

Dan L.note: Current position inferred from 2025-2026 PubMed affiliations; no official staff page found. A 2026 temsirolimus paper by 'Lifeng Dan' (Chongqing urology) is a different person and was not used. Previous profile used 'him'; pronoun removed because no source states it.

Chresta CM.lab_name: Oncology iMed, AstraZeneca, Alderley Park (Macclesfield, England, United Kingdom)
Chresta CM.role: Cancer biologist at AstraZeneca who led the preclinical description of AZD8055, one of the first ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors to reach clinical testing
Chresta CM.sub: Oncology iMed, AstraZeneca, Alderley Park (PubMed affiliation 2009–2016, at the time of the study) · School of Biological Sciences, University of Manchester (1996, with John Hickman)
story: Rapamycin does not block mTOR completely. It sticks to the side of the enzyme and blocks only some outputs of mTORC1, and it leaves mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, largely untouched. Christine Chresta was first author of the 2009 Cancer Research paper in this Atlas (CHR2009) that described AZD8055, a drug that plugs the ATP pocket of mTOR, the site where the enzyme takes up its energy source. AZD8055 therefore blocks both complexes, including the outputs that resist rapamycin. In cancer cells and in mouse tumour models it slowed growth. The result was in cells and animals, not patients.

Chresta was one of the AstraZeneca scientists on a 2009 Biochemical Journal paper with Dario Alessi's group in Dundee describing Ku-0063794, another selective mTOR kinase inhibitor, and on a 2012 study combining AZD8055 with the MEK inhibitor selumetinib in mouse models of lung and colorectal cancer.

Earlier, at the University of Manchester, Chresta worked with John Hickman on how p53 and apoptosis, the cell's programmed death, shape the response of tumours to chemotherapy (1996 and 1999). Later AstraZeneca papers place the author in Oncology iMed at Alderley Park, working on molecular subtypes of lung and colorectal cancer (2013 to 2016). A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.CHR2009: First author: described AZD8055, an ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor that blocks both mTORC1 and mTORC2 and slows tumour growth in mice.

Chresta CM.note: No official current profile found; last confirmed AstraZeneca affiliation is 2016. The 2009 Dundee paper (Ku-0063794, PMID 19402821) is now tied to Chresta through co-authors Cosulich and AstraZeneca; curator may add it to her timeline if it is in the Atlas.

Cosulich S.lab_name: Oncology R&D, AstraZeneca (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Cosulich S.role: Cancer drug discovery scientist at AstraZeneca whose work spans PI3K and mTOR pathway inhibitors, PARP1 inhibitors and phosphoinositide lipid signalling
Cosulich S.sub: Oncology R&D, AstraZeneca, Cambridge (PubMed affiliation 2019–2026; Projects Group, 2022) · AstraZeneca, Alderley Park, Macclesfield (2009–2016)
story: Cancer cells can escape mTOR-blocking drugs by mutating mTOR itself. Sabina Cosulich is a co-author of the 2016 Nature paper in this Atlas (ROD2016), led from Memorial Sloan Kettering and UCSF, which found such mutations in breast cancer cells treated with mTOR inhibitors. Some mutations raised mTOR's own activity. The team then built RapaLink-1, a third-generation drug that joins rapamycin to an ATP-site inhibitor in one molecule, and showed in cells and mice that it still works against the resistant mutants. Cosulich was the AstraZeneca contributor on the author list.

Cosulich has worked on the mTOR pathway at AstraZeneca for many years. A 2009 Biochemical Journal paper with Dario Alessi's group in Dundee, describing the selective mTOR kinase inhibitor Ku-0063794, lists Sabina C. Cosulich together with AstraZeneca colleague Christine Chresta.

Later papers place Cosulich in AstraZeneca Oncology R&D in Cambridge, UK: on a 2019 review and a 2025 study with the Babraham Institute about the fatty-acid make-up of phosphoinositides, the membrane lipids that PI3K signalling uses, on the 2022 preclinical description of the PARP1 inhibitor AZD5305, and on a 2026 paper about a TEAD inhibitor for Hippo-pathway cancers.

highlights.ROD2016: Co-author: AstraZeneca contributor to the study that found mTOR resistance mutations and designed RapaLink-1 to overcome them.

Cosulich S.note: Current position based on 2026 PubMed affiliation (AstraZeneca, Cambridge); no official profile page found. Previous profile used 'her'; pronoun removed because no source states it.

Kraig E.lab_name: Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Kraig E.role: Immunologist at UT Health San Antonio who studies how aging changes immune regulation and who led the first small safety trial of rapamycin in healthy older people at the Barshop Institute
Kraig E.sub: Professor and Deputy Chair of Faculty Development, Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, UT Health San Antonio · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · Distinguished Fellow, American Association of Immunologists · postdoc, Leroy Hood lab, Caltech · PhD, Brandeis University (Jim Haber lab)
story: Before anyone can test whether rapamycin slows human aging, someone has to show that healthy older people can take it safely. Ellen Kraig was first author of the 2018 trial in this Atlas (KRA2018) that asked this question. Twenty-five healthy adults aged 70 to 95 took low-dose rapamycin or a placebo every day for at least 8 weeks. The drug was generally well tolerated. There were small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. The trial was small and short, so it says nothing about long-term benefit, but it was early groundwork for larger aging trials.

Kraig trained in genetics and immunology. As a graduate student at Brandeis University in Jim Haber's lab she studied mating type in yeast, and she then joined Leroy Hood's lab at Caltech as a postdoc. At UT Health San Antonio she is Professor and Deputy Chair of Faculty Development in the Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy. Her research uses molecular and cellular assays to study how aging affects immune regulation, work developed with colleagues at the Barshop Institute. She has also won several teaching awards, including a 2018 Regents' Outstanding Teaching Award, and was named a Distinguished Fellow of the American Association of Immunologists.

The question from the pilot trial continues. In 2026 UT Health San Antonio announced a larger randomized, placebo-controlled study of rapamycin and everolimus in about 84 healthy adults aged 65 to 90, co-led by Kraig with Dean Kellogg Jr. and Brett Ginsburg, to work out dosing and short-term effects in older people.

highlights.KRA2018: First author: ran the randomized pilot trial showing that daily low-dose rapamycin was well tolerated by healthy adults aged 70 to 95 over 8 weeks.

Kraig E.note: Pronoun 'she/her' taken from the UT Health Regents' award page (first person) and Texas Biomed-style news; the Regents page is written in first person, so pronoun use kept minimal. lab_url is the UT System award page, not a lab page.

Musi N.lab_name: Diabetes and Aging Center, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Musi N.role: Endocrinologist and aging researcher who directs the Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism and the Diabetes and Aging Center at Cedars-Sinai, and who studies how aging drives insulin resistance, frailty and senescence
Musi N.sub: Director, Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, and Director, Diabetes and Aging Center, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (since 2022) · Kathi and Gary Cypres Chair in Diabetes Research (2024) · earlier at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio, and South Texas Veterans Health Care System (PubMed affiliation 2018)
story: Nicolas Musi is a co-author of the 2018 trial in this Atlas (KRA2018), a randomized placebo-controlled pilot study in 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95. Daily low-dose rapamycin for at least 8 weeks was generally well tolerated, with small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. That last point mattered to a diabetes researcher, because rapamycin can disturb sugar handling in mice. The trial was small and short.

At the time Musi worked at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies and the Department of Medicine of UT Health San Antonio, and at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System. His research covers how aging affects metabolism and cells in diabetes, obesity and sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss), the effects of exercise on glucose and fat metabolism, and cellular senescence, the state in which damaged cells stop dividing but stay active.

Musi moved to Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles in 2022. There he directs the Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism and the Diabetes and Aging Center, and in 2024 became the first holder of the Kathi and Gary Cypres Chair in Diabetes Research. His current work includes a clinical trial testing whether removing senescent cells improves glucose metabolism and physical function. He is an elected member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research.

highlights.KRA2018: Co-author: part of the San Antonio team that ran the pilot safety trial of daily rapamycin in healthy adults aged 70 to 95.

Musi N.note: Pronoun 'his' from the Cedars-Sinai newsroom page. Training (MD school, fellowship) not found in an official source. ZHO2001 (initial N only) still not linked.

Fernandez E.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Fernandez E.role: Aging researcher at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio who has worked on rapamycin studies in mice and common marmosets, including the NIA Interventions Testing Program
Fernandez E.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio, and Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System (PubMed affiliation 2014–2026) · Department of Pharmacology, UT Health San Antonio
story: Rapamycin lengthens life in mice, but mice are far from people. Elizabeth Fernandez is a co-author of two Atlas studies that tried the drug in the common marmoset, a small, short-lived monkey. The 2014 study (TAR2014) worked out how to give rapamycin by mouth in a coated form, reached blood levels similar to those in mouse and human work, and saw lower mTORC1 signalling, the growth-control pathway, in the animals' tissues. The 2015 study (ROS2015) found that long-term treatment had only minor effects on body weight, activity, blood fats and glucose handling. Neither study measured lifespan.

Fernandez is also a co-author of a 2022 report from the NIA Interventions Testing Program (STR2022), which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Rapamycin combined with acarbose, a diabetes drug, gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone had in earlier cohorts. In females the combination was no better than rapamycin alone.

PubMed places Fernandez at the Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio, and at the Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center of the South Texas Veterans Health Care System on papers from 2014 to 2026. A 2026 paper with Randy Strong found that long-term rapamycin protected aging mice against the decline in motor function, with a larger effect in females. A current job title could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.TAR2014: Co-author: part of the team that first described oral rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in common marmosets.
highlights.ROS2015: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that long-term rapamycin had only minor metabolic effects in marmosets.
highlights.STR2022: Co-author: contributed to the Interventions Testing Program report in which rapamycin plus acarbose extended male mouse lifespan beyond rapamycin alone.

Fernandez E.note: No official profile found. Previous profile used 'her'; pronoun removed because no source states it. Five more Atlas records under this name lack PubMed affiliation and remain unlinked.

Lelegren M.lab_name: Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System, and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Lelegren M.role: First author of a 2016 study of how rapamycin changes the protein-quality-control machinery in marmoset liver, muscle and fat, carried out in Adam Salmon's group in San Antonio
Lelegren M.sub: Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, South Texas Veterans Health Care System, and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (at the time of the study, 2016)
story: Cells keep their proteins in good shape with a set of systems called the proteostasis network. Proteasomes chop up damaged proteins, chaperones help proteins fold, and autophagy recycles larger pieces of the cell. Blocking mTOR is thought to boost some of these systems, which may be part of how rapamycin slows aging in mice.

Matthew Lelegren was first author of the 2016 Atlas study (LEL2016) that checked this idea in a primate, using tissue from common marmosets treated with rapamycin in an earlier pilot. In liver and muscle, rapamycin went with more of PSMB5, a core proteasome subunit, but proteasome activity did not change. Chaperones that work inside mitochondria rose in muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in muscle and fat but not liver. Only parts of the network responded, and differently in each tissue. The samples came from a small group of animals, and the changes are protein levels, not proven effects on health.

The work was done at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System and the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, with Adam Salmon as senior author. No later research paper tied to this person could be confirmed, so the current position is not known.

highlights.LEL2016: First author: measured proteasome, chaperone and autophagy markers in rapamycin-treated marmoset tissues and found tissue-specific changes.

Lelegren M.note: PubMed lists a Matthew (J.) Lelegren in Otolaryngology at Eastern Virginia Medical School, Norfolk (2020-2022, PMIDs 33170026, 33934006, 35985081). The name is rare and the career path (research in San Antonio, then medical training) is plausible, but there is no shared institution or co-author, so it was NOT used. Curator may want to confirm.
